title: Benchmarking the Quantum Leap: Auditing LLM Evaluation for Quantum Code Generation
title_zh: 基准测试量子飞跃：审计量子代码生成中的 LLM 评估

paragraphs.en: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of generating quantum programs, but reliable evaluation remains difficult: benchmarks differ in task composition, scoring procedures, and failure handling, while leaderboard rankings can obscure uncertainty and evaluator defects. We evaluate 15 hosted frontier, open-weight, quantum-specialized, and retrieval-augmented models across five primary quantum code-generation suites containing 530 tasks, and 10 models on QuantumBenchEval (QBE), a new benchmark of 96 tasks across six quantum-computing topics that we introduce. We report task-level bootstrap confidence intervals, multiplicity-adjusted paired comparisons, and audits of evaluator behavior, output validity, and shared failures. QiskitHumanEval-Standard is approaching saturation for the strongest models (98.7% pass@1), whereas its Hard variant retains substantial headroom (63.8%); across the recorded primary-suite outcomes, none of the five top-two comparisons remains significant after multiple-comparison correction. Evaluation design can have an even larger effect: removing checks on quantities the prompts never specified in two QuantumBenchEval topics raises GPT-6 Astra’s pass@1 from 0% to 94.1% (T1) and from 1.2% to 92.9% (T6) without changing its outputs. Our audit also identifies 17 QuanBench-117 tasks with shared failures associated with benchmark-owned imports, while controlled probes of the current evaluator reveal unexecuted unit tests, leakage of canonical functions into candidate execution, and reference imports that can block otherwise valid candidates. These defects can affect both apparent failures and apparent passes, requiring historical QuanBench outcomes to be revalidated under an isolated evaluator. Together, these results show that quantum code-generation progress cannot be characterized by leaderboard scores alone. We release the evaluation harness, per-sample outcomes, and audit artifacts, and advocate protocols that validate scoring and test execution, isolate candidate and reference code, report uncertainty and output validity, and respect sampling assumptions when estimating pass@ k k .
paragraphs.zh: 大型语言模型（LLM）日益具备生成量子程序的能力，但可靠的评估仍然困难：各基准测试在任务构成、评分流程和失败处理上各不相同，而排行榜排名可能掩盖不确定性和评估器的缺陷。 我们在五个包含 530 个任务的主要量子代码生成套件上评估了 15 个托管前沿模型、开源权重模型、量子专用模型和检索增强模型，并在 QuantumBenchEval（QBE）上评估了 10 个模型——QBE 是我们推出的一个新基准，包含横跨六个量子计算主题的 96 个任务。 我们报告了任务级自助法置信区间、经多重性校正的配对比较，以及对评估器行为、输出有效性和共同失败的审计。 QiskitHumanEval-Standard 对最强模型已接近饱和（98.7% pass@1），而其 Hard 变体仍有较大提升空间（63.8%）；在记录的主要套件结果中，五组前二名比较经过多重比较校正后均不再显著。 评估设计可能产生更大的影响：在 QuantumBenchEval 的两个主题中，移除对提示词从未规定之量的检查后，GPT-6 Astra 的 pass@1 从 0% 升至 94.1%（T1），从 1.2% 升至 92.9%（T6），而其输出并未改变。 我们的审计还发现 QuanBench-117 中有 17 个任务存在与基准自带导入相关的共同失败，而对当前评估器的受控探测则揭示了未执行的单元测试、规范函数泄漏到候选代码执行中，以及可能阻断本有效候选代码的参考导入。 这些缺陷既可能影响表面的失败，也可能影响表面的通过，因此需要对历史 QuanBench 结果在隔离评估器下进行重新验证。 综合来看，这些结果表明量子代码生成的进展无法仅凭排行榜分数来刻画。 我们发布了评估框架、逐样本结果和审计工件，并倡导以下协议：验证评分与测试执行、隔离候选代码与参考代码、报告不确定性与输出有效性，并在估计 pass@k 时尊重采样假设。

paragraphs.en: A programmer asked to prepare a four-qubit W state, or to decompose a CNOT into iSWAP gates, must reason about circuit semantics, measurement statistics, and backend constraints in addition to ordinary concerns of API usage and correctness ( Riofrío et al., 2025 ) . Large language models (LLMs) have become capable code generators ( Chen et al., 2021 ) , and several systems now target this setting directly, including Qiskit Code Assistant ( Dupuis et al., 2024 ) , QSpark ( Kheiri et al., 2025 ) , PennyCoder ( Basit et al., 2025b ) , and Agent-Q ( Jern et al., 2025 ) . A parallel line of work has produced benchmarks for measuring them, from Qiskit HumanEval ( Vishwakarma et al., 2024 ) and QCircuitNet ( Yang et al., 2024 ) to QHackBench ( Basit et al., 2025c ) , QCoder ( Mikuriya et al., 2025 ) , and QuanBench ( Guo et al., 2025 ) .

paragraphs.en: These benchmarks do not agree on what to measure or how. They differ in task composition, execution environment, and output format. Some grade by executable unit tests; others require a model-based judge or a custom scoring function. Three consequences follow for anyone comparing models across them. First, a suite may lose discriminative power as models improve, so that a leaderboard position no longer distinguishes capability. Second, a difference between two models may be smaller than the sampling noise of a few hundred tasks, so that leaderboard order and statistical evidence for separation come apart. Third, a benchmark score depends on the reference solutions, test harness, dependencies, and evaluator assumptions as much as on the generated program, so that a defect in any of these components is misread as a failure, or a success, of the model. Systematic analysis of evaluation validity of this kind exists for classical code generation ( Chen et al., 2021 ) but not, to our knowledge, for quantum code generation.
paragraphs.zh: 这些基准测试在测什么、怎么测上并不一致。 它们在任务构成、执行环境和输出格式上各不相同。 有些通过可执行的单元测试评分；另一些则需要基于模型的裁判或自定义的评分函数。 对于任何在这些基准之间比较模型的人来说，会产生三个后果。 首先，随着模型能力的提升，某个测试套件可能会失去区分能力，以致排行榜上的位置不再能区分能力高低。 其次，两个模型之间的差异可能小于几百个任务带来的采样噪声，以致排行榜的排序与区分性的统计证据相互脱节。 第三，基准分数不仅取决于生成的程序，同样取决于参考答案、测试框架、依赖项和评估器的假设，以致其中任何组件的缺陷都会被误读为模型的失败或成功。 对这类评估有效性的系统分析在经典代码生成领域已有（Chen 等，2021），但据我们所知，在量子代码生成领域尚属空白。

paragraphs.en: In this paper, we ask two questions: how well do current LLMs generate quantum code, and how reliably do existing protocols measure that ability? We evaluate 15 models spanning hosted frontier, open-weight, quantum-specialized, and retrieval-augmented systems on five established suites comprising 530 tasks. We also introduce QuantumBenchEval (QBE), a new 96-task benchmark spanning six quantum-computing topics, on which we evaluate 10 models. Because its tasks are newly constructed, they are less likely than long-standing public suites to appear in training data. Across all suites we report uncertainty, statistical separability, shared failures, output validity, and evaluator behavior rather than point estimates alone.

paragraphs.en: A benchmark score measures a model only if the evaluator measures the intended capability, and a growing body of work shows that it often does not. Liu et al. (2023) found that HumanEval’s unit tests are too sparse to catch many incorrect programs; augmenting them substantially lowers pass@ k k and reorders models. Benchmark-side defects also cause false failures: SWE-bench ( Jimenez et al., 2023 ) was refined into a human-validated Verified subset after annotators found tasks whose issue descriptions were underspecified or whose tests rejected valid solutions. Contamination is a third threat, which LiveCodeBench ( Jain et al., 2025 ) and MathArena ( Balunovic et al., 2026 ) address by evaluating on problems released after model training; MathArena also reports inflated performance on older, widely circulated competitions. Where no executable oracle exists, LLM judges are a common substitute, but Zheng et al. (2023) document position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases in such judges. Finally, small benchmarks call for explicit uncertainty: Miller (2024) argues for task-level confidence intervals and paired comparisons in place of raw leaderboard ordering. The quantum code-generation benchmarks above report single-suite leaderboards without auditing their evaluators. We apply these validity concerns to quantum code generation, where each one appears: tests that never execute and reference-side imports that block valid candidates (§ 4.5 ), scoring contracts that check undisclosed quantities (§ 4.4 ), a judge-scored suite with a non-i.i.d. protocol (§ 4.6 ), and top-model differences that do not survive multiplicity correction (§ 4.2 ).
paragraphs.zh: 只有当评测器确实测量了目标能力时，基准分数才能衡量一个模型，而越来越多的研究表明情况往往并非如此。Liu 等人 (2023) 发现 HumanEval 的单元测试过于稀疏，无法捕获许多错误的程序；对这些测试加以扩充后，pass@k 大幅下降，且模型的排名顺序发生改变。 基准侧的缺陷也会导致假性失败：SWE-bench（Jimenez 等人，2023）在标注者发现某些任务的议题描述不明确或其测试会拒绝正确解之后，被精炼为经过人工校验的 Verified 子集。 数据污染是第三种威胁，LiveCodeBench（Jain 等人，2025）和 MathArena（Balunovic 等人，2026）通过在模型训练之后发布的问题上进行评测来应对这一威胁；MathArena 还报告了模型在较早的、广泛流传的竞赛题目上性能被夸大的现象。 在不存在可执行判准的情况下，大语言模型裁判是常见的替代方案，但 Zheng 等人 (2023) 记录了此类裁判中存在的位置、冗长和自我偏好偏差。 最后，小型基准需要显式的不确定性度量：Miller (2024) 主张用任务级别的置信区间和配对比较来取代原始的排行榜排序。 上述量子代码生成基准报告的单一测试套件排行榜，均未对其评测器进行审计。 我们将这些效度问题应用于量子代码生成，其中每一个问题都会出现：从不执行的测试以及阻止有效候选解的参考侧导入（§ 4.5），检查未公开量的评分契约（§ 4.4），采用非独立同分布协议的由裁判评分的测试套件（§ 4.6），以及在多重性校正后无法保持的头部模型差异（§ 4.2）。

paragraphs.en: We evaluate models across five quantum programming benchmarks spanning two evaluation paradigms: execution-based correctness and LLM-based judgment.
paragraphs.zh: 我们在五个量子编程基准上评估模型，涵盖两种评估范式：基于执行的正确性和基于 LLM 的评判。

paragraphs.en: QiskitHumanEval (Standard, 151 tasks) is a quantum adaptation of the HumanEval benchmark, consisting of short programming problems covering core quantum computing primitives such as state preparation, circuit construction, and measurement. Correctness is determined via unit tests.
paragraphs.zh: QiskitHumanEval（标准版，151 个任务）是 HumanEval 基准的量子适配版本，由简短的编程题目组成，涵盖状态准备、线路构建和测量等核心量子计算原语。 正确性通过单元测试来判定。

paragraphs.en: QiskitHumanEval (Hard, 151 tasks) is a difficulty-enhanced variant of the standard benchmark, requiring deeper compositional reasoning and multi-step circuit design.

paragraphs.en: QuanBench-117 (117 tasks) is a large-scale benchmark designed to cover a broad spectrum of quantum programming concepts, emphasizing generalization across diverse tasks.
paragraphs.zh: QuanBench-117（117 个任务）是一个大规模基准，旨在覆盖广泛的量子编程概念，强调在多样化任务上的泛化能力。

paragraphs.en: QuanBench-44 (44 tasks) is a smaller subset of QuanBench that enables controlled comparison under reduced task diversity.
paragraphs.zh: QuanBench-44（44 个任务）是 QuanBench 的一个较小子集，用于在降低任务多样性的条件下进行受控比较。

paragraphs.en: QCoder (67 tasks) consists of open-ended quantum programming problems without canonical solutions or executable test cases. These tasks emphasize end-to-end reasoning and algorithmic design rather than test-driven correctness.

paragraphs.en: QCoder provides no executable tests, so each candidate receives a binary PASS/FAIL verdict from an LLM judge (per-run judge identities in Appendix A.2 ). Claude Opus 4.6 is excluded from the QCoder roster to avoid self-evaluation; Claude Fable 5.1 shares a provider with the QCoder and T3 judges and was retained, so its judge-scored results are flagged given documented self-preference effects ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) .

T3 contains 15 tasks requiring Qiskit implementations of variational ground-state energy estimation for molecular and lattice systems. Because multiple implementations can be valid, T3 has no binary outcome. Each judged sample is scored on a fixed 10-point rubric: energy accuracy (3), chemical accuracy (1), required outputs (2), qubit and circuit specification (2), and scientific reasoning (2). Candidate code runs in an isolated subprocess; energy accuracy is recomputed deterministically from the executed energy against a task-specific reference, and the remaining criteria are scored by Claude Sonnet 4.6 from the candidate code and execution result.

We report valid-output rates (nonempty and syntactically valid, with total-sample denominators), rule-based classifications of saved evaluation errors, and observed task coverage (empirical pass@5) with pairwise complementarity. Union coverage is an oracle quantity that uses additional generation budget, not a deployable selector. We also compute CodeBLEU ( Ren et al., 2020 ) and its per-sample point-biserial correlation with pass/fail. None of these diagnostics establishes functional or quantum-semantic correctness. Error-label definitions, CodeBLEU scoring details, T1 resource closeness, token usage, and incomplete-run bounds are given in Appendix A.3 .

We evaluate current language models across the five primary quantum code-generation suites described in Section 3 , and separately analyze QuantumBenchEval (QBE) as an evaluator-focused benchmark. Unless otherwise stated, results are reported as pass@1 with pointwise 95% task-bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 replicates. We emphasize task-level uncertainty and paired comparisons rather than interpreting raw leaderboard ordering as evidence of model separation. QuanBench results are retained as recorded evaluator outcomes but require replay following the evaluator audit described in Section 4.5 .

Table 2 summarizes pass@1 across the five primary suites. Performance varies substantially across benchmarks, and no single ordering describes all five evaluations. QiskitHumanEval Standard is particularly concentrated at the top: GPT-6 Astra reaches 98.7% pass@1 [96.7–100.0], Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview reaches 97.6% [95.1–99.6], and Muse-Glimmer-30B reaches 95.1% [92.5–97.5]. The corresponding Hard split remains considerably less saturated, with the highest recorded pass@1 at 63.8% [56.4–71.0].

QuanBench exhibits a different ordering. Claude Fable 5.1 records the highest pass@1 on QuanBench-44 at 60.0% [45.9–73.6], while several systems cluster near 84–85% on QuanBench-117. These QuanBench values should not be interpreted as validated capability estimates, however, because our evaluator audit identifies defects affecting both apparent passes and apparent failures (Section 4.5 ).

QCoder produces another distinct performance profile. Among complete runs, Claude Fable 5.1 records 43.0% pass@1 [33.7–52.2], followed by GPT-6 Astra at 32.8% [25.4–40.6]. Because QCoder conditions later generations on prior attempts, these pass@ k k values describe the recorded sequential protocol rather than an unbiased independent-sampling estimator.

The Standard and Hard QiskitHumanEval suites provide a useful contrast in remaining benchmark headroom. Across five attempts per model, only one of the 151 Standard tasks is unsolved by every evaluated model, compared with 31 of 151 Hard tasks. The highest observed pass@1 correspondingly falls from 98.7% on Standard to 63.8% on Hard. All 15 models record lower pass@1 on the Hard split, although we treat this as a benchmark-level contrast rather than a causal estimate of difficulty because task-ID correspondence alone does not establish a controlled paired intervention.

Raw leaderboard ordering also overstates how strongly the evaluated suites separate their highest-scoring systems. Table 3 reports the two highest observed pass@1 values on each suite together with paired task-level differences. After Holm correction within each suite, none of the five top-two gaps is significant. On Hard and QCoder the unadjusted evidence is suggestive ( p = 0.016 p{=}0.016 and 0.003 0.003 ; the paired intervals exclude zero), but it does not survive correction for the full set of within-suite comparisons. An observed first place therefore should not be read as evidence that the leading model is reliably better than the runner-up.

Suite choice also changes the ordering itself. Pass@1 rank agreement is high among most execution-scored suites (Spearman ρ \rho 0.78–0.89) but only ρ = 0.54 \rho{=}0.54 between QiskitHumanEval-Standard and QCoder (Appendix A.4 ), so no single suite recovers the cross-suite ranking. Additional samples do not separate the leaders either: the strongest models gain at most about 6 pp from pass@1 to pass@5 on the execution-scored suites (zero for GPT-6 Astra on three of four), whereas quantum-specialized models gain up to 38 pp and reorder the lower half of the leaderboard (Appendix D.2 ).

Observed coverage reinforces the difference between the suites without implying that any task is intrinsically unsolvable. Across the available roster, the number of tasks unsolved in all five recorded attempts is 1/151 for Standard, 31/151 for Hard, 9/44 for QuanBench-44, 17/117 for QuanBench-117, and 12/67 for QCoder. These are empirical coverage statistics, equivalent to observed pass@5 coverage across the roster, rather than estimates of a fundamental capability ceiling.

Figure 1 reports pass@1 across the ten shared QiskitHumanEval task categories for Standard and Hard. Standard is broadly saturated among the strongest models: GPT-6 Astra reaches 100% pass@1 in eight of ten categories, with the remaining two at 96.0% and 95.2%.

Hard reveals substantially greater category-level variation. For Astra, pass@1 ranges from 20.0% on Quantum Information and 44.8% on Backend and Runtime to 75.0% on Quantum Circuit Generation and 85.7% on State Preparation and Analysis ; similar heterogeneity appears across other strong models. Because category sizes range from 5 to 28 tasks, these results are interpreted descriptively rather than as a secondary model ranking.

QuantumBenchEval (QBE) complements the established suites with 96 new tasks spanning six quantum-computing topics. Instead of short API-completion problems, its tasks are multi-step scientific workflows that require reasoning about algorithm design, resource use, optimization, simulation, and scientific outputs. Each task is scored by its own evaluator, and because the tasks are newly constructed, they are less likely than long-standing public suites to appear in model training data.

Figure 2 shows substantial variation across both models and topics. The hosted frontier models score above zero on several topics, while the smaller open-weight and quantum-specialized systems score zero pass@1 on every assertion-scored topic. We do not read these zeros as an absence of quantum knowledge. The same models receive nonzero T3 rubric scores (1.1–2.0 of 10), so the zeros more plausibly reflect failure to produce complete outputs in the required structure than failure to engage with the task. Among the stronger systems, performance is highly topic dependent. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 both reach 94.1% pass@1 on corrected T1, yet score 40.0% [22.4–58.8] and 82.4% [69.4–94.1] on T5. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview reaches 83.5% [76.5–90.6] on T5, while no model exceeds 32% on T4. The six topics therefore probe different capabilities, and no single model ordering holds across them.

We applied the same audit to our own evaluators, checking whether each scoring rule matches the information given to the model. It flagged three topics. T1’s evaluator checked exact resource quantities the prompts never specified, and T6’s required a scalar reproducibility value whose form the prompts never stated. Removing only these checks, while keeping every correctness check and rescoring the saved outputs, raises GPT-6 Astra from 0% to 94.1% on T1 and from 1.2% to 92.9% on T6; on T6 this moves it from last to first among the frontier models. All 32 reference solutions pass under both evaluators, and no replayed sample changes from pass to fail (Appendix C.4 ). T2 also checks undisclosed evaluation counts, but removing them changes little (at most 13.3% pass@1 on the 12 internally consistent tasks), and three T2 tasks contain data that contradict their required answers, so we report T2 as recorded. T3 is scored differently again, as a rubric mean over judged samples rather than pass@1.

The 17 QuanBench-117 tasks unsolved across the observed roster initially appear to form a shared performance ceiling. Inspection instead identifies a common benchmark-side obstruction: for each of the 17 tasks, the dominant recorded failure corresponds to an import in benchmark-owned reference or test code, including dependencies from qiskit_algorithms , qiskit_optimization , qiskit.primitives , and qiskit_machine_learning .This does not imply that every candidate on these tasks is correct (some outputs fail before reaching the shared obstruction), but it prevents some outputs fail before reaching the shared obstruction, but it prevents the observed ceiling from being interpreted as a pure model-capability limit.

More importantly, source inspection and controlled synthetic probes identify three defects in the current QuanBench evaluator. First, the evaluator executes test scripts without explicitly loading and running their unittest test cases; all 117 current QuanBench-117 scripts contain test classes and no top-level expression calls. A deliberately incorrect candidate therefore passes when the failing assertion is confined to such a test class. Second, canonical code is executed in the candidate namespace before generated code, allowing an empty candidate to satisfy an explicit assertion by inheriting the canonical function. Third, a valid synthetic candidate can fail before execution when the canonical solution imports a missing dependency. The false-pass mechanism is not only hypothetical: a recorded QuanBench-117 pass (Task 110, Claude Opus 4.6) returns a circuit that is not equivalent to CNOT up to global phase (Appendix E ).

These controlled probes demonstrate mechanisms for both false passes and false failures. Historical evaluator source was not immutably captured, so they do not prove that every saved QuanBench outcome was produced by the exact inspected revision. We therefore retain the historical scores as recorded evaluator outcomes and require replay of unchanged candidates under a versioned, isolated evaluator before interpreting either successes or failures as validated capability estimates. QuanBench-44 has a different test-script structure, so the class-only finding for QuanBench-117 is not automatically extended to every QuanBench-44 task.

QCoder evaluates open-ended programs with a model-based judge rather than executable unit tests. Among complete evaluations, Claude Fable 5.1 § records 43.0% pass@1 [33.7–52.2] and 67.2% observed pass@5 [55.2–77.6], while GPT-6 Astra records 32.8% pass@1 [25.4–40.6] and the same 67.2% observed pass@5. Equal coverage does not mean identical behavior: each model solves 45/67 tasks within five attempts, with 40 shared successes and five unique successes each, so their oracle union covers 50/67 tasks (74.6%). This shows complementary observed coverage, not a demonstrated ensemble, since combining the systems doubles the generation budget and relies on oracle knowledge of which candidate succeeds.

These results are also conditioned on the generation configuration. GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Muse-Glimmer-30B produced no usable code under a 2,048-token output limit, so their runs used 32,768 tokens. Earlier runs, including GPT-5, used 2,048, and GPT-5’s 63% empty-output rate on QCoder shows that the cap was binding for it as well (Appendix D.4 ). The judge also changed between the two groups ( claude-sonnet-4 before April 2026, claude-sonnet-4-6 after), and neither group was re-judged with the other judge. Gaps between the earlier and later runs therefore reflect model capability together with output budget and judge version, and the within-group comparison of Fable and Astra is the most controlled one QCoder provides.

Muse-Glimmer-30B is provisional: it has completed 45/67 tasks (completed-subset pass@1 53.3%; full-dataset bounds 35.8–68.7%, obtained by assigning every unfinished task failure or success) and is excluded from QCoder rankings.

Our results show that measured quantum code-generation performance depends as much on how correctness is operationalized as on the model evaluated. Correcting one QBE evaluator changes two models’ pass@1 by 94.1 pp on unchanged outputs; the current QuanBench evaluator admits both false passes and false failures; and no primary suite separates its top two models after multiplicity correction. Meanwhile QiskitHumanEval-Standard is near saturation, so headroom now lies in harder or less-exposed tasks such as the Hard split and QBE.

These effects compound. A leaderboard entry for QuanBench-117 reflects the model, its output budget, whether the evaluator runs its tests, and whether reference code leaks into the candidate namespace; a QCoder entry additionally reflects the judge version. Comparisons are most trustworthy within a single configuration and evaluator revision, as with Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra on QCoder. Across configurations, differences smaller than the evaluator effects documented here should not be interpreted as capability differences.

Quantum code benchmarks should (i) validate reference solutions and confirm that tests execute under the released harness; (ii) isolate candidate code from reference code; (iii) disclose every quantity the scorer checks; (iv) report valid-output rates alongside pass@ k k ; (v) report uncertainty and corrected paired comparisons rather than raw ordering; and (vi) use independent sampling whenever pass@ k k is estimated.

QuanBench outcomes await replay under an isolated evaluator. QBE T2 contracts are corrected only in the release, and T1/T6 rescoring used replay on a different platform (5 of 1,600 samples differ). QCoder uses a non-i.i.d. protocol, its judge changed between runs, and all judges share a provider with one evaluated model. Decoding settings and output budgets differ across models, and our roster reflects one point in time.

In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with implementing portions of the initial analysis and evaluation code and with developing and refining the statistical analysis framework, including bootstrap confidence intervals, paired comparisons, and multiple-comparison correction. We did not use generative AI tools to generate synthetic datasets, formulate or prove mathematical claims, clean or reformat datasets, perform qualitative or thematic data analysis, or translate research materials; the remaining required-disclosure tasks were not applicable to this work.

Additionally, we used generative AI tools to draft and edit portions of the manuscript for clarity, organization, and readability, and to assist with creating and editing research software. All AI-assisted code and statistical analyses were reviewed and tested by the authors, and reported results were verified against the underlying experimental outputs and evaluation artifacts. All AI-assisted manuscript text was reviewed and revised by the authors. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, code, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

This work evaluates language models on quantum code-generation benchmarks and does not involve human subjects, personally identifiable information, or sensitive personal data. We use benchmark data and model outputs solely for research evaluation and report known limitations, missing results, and evaluator defects rather than presenting provisional measurements as validated capability estimates. Released benchmark materials, model outputs, evaluation artifacts, and code will be distributed in accordance with applicable licenses and terms of use. We are not aware of additional ethical concerns arising from the experiments presented in this work.

All code, evaluation scripts, model configurations, prompts, and experimental results will be made publicly available upon acceptance. The datasets and models evaluated in this work are publicly available, and the paper and supplementary materials describe the benchmark construction, evaluation protocol, and experimental settings required to reproduce our results. We will additionally maintain a public version of the Quantum Arena containing links to the datasets, models, benchmark tasks, and detailed evaluation results. The arena is intended to support continued evaluation beyond this work, and we welcome additional model submissions to maintain the benchmark as a long-term, continuously updated quantum-computing leaderboard.

A single-suite leaderboard therefore recovers only part of the cross-suite ordering. The following examples illustrate the task interfaces and requested behaviors of the five primary suites. Descriptions are condensed from the repository prompts; task identifiers and function names are retained. The matched Standard and Hard examples illustrate a difference in prompt scaffolding, not a change in the underlying task. QuantumBenchEval is presented separately.
Task: Generate a quantum circuit containing a specified number of qubits.
Function signature: def create_quantum_circuit(n_qubits):
Description: Return a Qiskit quantum circuit with n_qubits qubits. The Standard prompt supplies the QuantumCircuit import and a function skeleton with a docstring describing the task.
Recorded test contract: The test calls the function with n_qubits=3 and checks that the result is a QuantumCircuit containing three qubits.
Required interface: def create_quantum_circuit(n_qubits):

Description: The Hard prompt states the task in natural language and specifies the function name and argument. It does not supply the import or Python function skeleton provided by the matched Standard prompt; the model must produce these itself.

Recorded test contract: For this matched example, the checks remain the same: the returned object must be a QuantumCircuit with three qubits when called with argument three. Thus, this example does not establish that Hard uses more demanding semantic checks.
Task: Implement Grover search for the marked state | 00 ⟩ \lvert 00\rangle .
Function signature: def grover_search_oracle_00() -> QuantumCircuit:
Description: Construct a Qiskit circuit implementing Grover search for | 00 ⟩ \lvert 00\rangle and return the circuit with measurements.

Intended checks in the saved test script: The test requests a comparison against the reference circuit using a KL-divergence helper, with a value in [ 0 , 0.05 ) [0,0.05) , and checks that 00 is the most frequent measurement outcome. These describe the saved assertions, not independently validated enforcement by the historical evaluator.
Function signature: def generate_quantum_state_qubit3() -> QuantumCircuit:
Description: Construct a Qiskit circuit that prepares the specified state and return the circuit with measurements.

Intended checks in the saved test script: Measurement outcomes must be restricted to 011 and 100 , with each observed frequency within 0.1 0.1 of 0.5 0.5 . A separate assertion requests a phase-helper value of π \pi for 100 , within 0.05 0.05 . The measurement-frequency check alone cannot establish the required relative phase.

For both QuanBench examples, the current evaluator audit found that executing these test-class definitions does not run their test methods. Reference-code leakage and reference-import failures provide additional failure mechanisms; the KL-divergence helpers also return a constant zero in the audited source. Accordingly, the checks above document intended test behavior, and should not be read as evidence that historical pass labels validate the requested quantum behavior. Historical outcomes require corrected, isolated replay.

All 96 QBE tasks were written by the authors for this work and were not published or shared before evaluation. Problem settings use standard scientific instances (e.g., textbook Hamiltonians and small graph problems) rather than items from existing benchmarks. Each task specifies a problem statement, a required function signature, the return fields the candidate must produce, a reference solution, an assertion suite (T3 excepted), and a common_failure_modes field written by the task author.
All 32 T2 and T6 reference solutions pass their assertion suites under both the original and corrected evaluators (Appendix C.4 ).

Our audit found scoring contracts that check quantities the prompts do not specify (T1 and T6, corrected and rescored; T2, reported as recorded), three T2 tasks ( t2_3 , t2_10 , t2_14 ) whose disclosed data contradict their required answers, and assertions that are too permissive (Appendix C.5 ). Task difficulty was not calibrated against human solvers, and topics are small (15–17 tasks), so per-topic intervals are wide.
QBE will be released with task files, reference solutions, assertion suites, the T3 rubric and judge prompt, and all saved outputs and scores under both the original and corrected evaluators.

QuantumBenchEval contains 96 tasks across six topics (Table 6 ). Each task specifies a required function signature and a list of required output fields. Tasks in T1, T2, T4, T5, and T6 are scored by executing the candidate and applying a task-specific assertion suite; T3 is scored with a rubric (Appendix C.3 ).

Each judged T3 sample is scored out of 10: energy accuracy (3 points), chemical accuracy (1), required outputs (2), qubit and circuit specification (2), and scientific reasoning (2). Candidate code runs in an isolated subprocess. Energy accuracy is recomputed deterministically from the executed energy against the task reference, and the remaining criteria are scored by claude-sonnet-4-6 . Truncated responses are neither executed nor judged and are excluded rather than scored zero. Table 7 reports the denominators.

T3 scores should be read as indicative rather than calibrated. (i) Seven of the ten rubric points are assigned by a single LLM judge ( claude-sonnet-4-6 ) in one pass; we did not measure inter-run agreement, agreement with a second judge, or agreement with human raters. (ii) The judge shares a provider with Claude Fable 5.1, the highest-scoring model on T3 ( § ), so self-preference cannot be ruled out. (iii) Means are conditional on judged samples, and denominators differ across models: Gemini 3.6 Flash is scored on 43 of 75 samples and Granite-Qiskit on none, so its means are not comparable to models judged on all 75. (iv) Only the 3-point energy-accuracy term is computed deterministically; the other criteria (required outputs, circuit specification, scientific reasoning) depend on the judge’s reading of code and execution output. (v) The rubric weights were set by the authors and not validated against expert rankings. A human-rated subset and a cross-provider judge would address (i)–(ii); we leave both to the released benchmark.

Before changing any evaluator, we audited every T2 and T6 assertion against its candidate-facing prompt, then applied a pre-declared minimal change. For T6, only the reproducibility assertion was removed, because no prompt defines its form; all partition-quality assertions are unchanged. For T2, only exact evaluation-count assertions were removed, and tasks t2_3 , t2_10 , and t2_14 were excluded as internally inconsistent (their disclosed data contradict their required answers). No selection encoding was normalized. Saved outputs were replayed without regeneration. All 32 reference solutions pass under both evaluators, and no paired sample changes from pass to fail. All 99 T6 flips come from samples whose first recorded failure was the reproducibility type check. The replay ran on x86_64, whereas the original runs used aarch64; 5 of 1,600 samples differ between historical and replayed original outcomes because of simulator stochasticity. One of these (Gemini 3.1 Pro, t6_8.3 ) fails an unchanged quality assertion under both evaluators.

Figure 8 shows, for each model pair, how many more tasks the oracle union of their solved sets covers than the better single model. Gains are modest (at most 11 pp on Hard and 7 pp on QCoder). On Hard they are largest for pairs involving quantum-specialized models (Muse-Glimmer-30B with Qwen-Qiskit, 11 pp; Mistral-Qiskit with Qwen-Qiskit, 9 pp), which suggests that specialized fine-tuning covers some tasks that general models miss. On QCoder the largest gain is between the two strongest models, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra (7 pp). Union coverage is an oracle quantity with double the generation budget; it is not the performance of a deployable ensemble.

Figure 9 shows the paired gain from pass@1 to pass@5. The strongest hosted models gain almost nothing on the execution-scored suites: GPT-6 Astra’s gain is exactly zero on Standard, QuanBench-44, and QuanBench-117, and Claude Fable 5.1’s is zero on QuanBench-117 despite sampling at temperature 1.0. For these models, the five samples per task almost always succeed or fail together, so pass@5 adds little beyond pass@1. Quantum-specialized and small open-weight models gain far more, up to 38 pp (Granite-Qiskit on QuanBench-117), which reorders several models between pass@1 and pass@5 (Appendix A.4 ). The Gemini Flash models also gain 21–25 pp on QuanBench-117, the suite on which their syntax-valid rate is lowest (Table 13 ). This pattern is consistent with intermittent formatting failures that additional samples recover, although we have not verified that cause. QCoder gains are largest for the strongest models (up to 34 pp for GPT-6 Astra). Because QCoder conditions each sample on the model’s prior attempts to diversify outputs, these gains are not comparable to those on the i.i.d. suites.

QCoder tasks have no canonical solutions or executable tests. Each candidate therefore receives a binary Pass / Fail verdict from an LLM judge given the problem statement and candidate code (Table 5 ). All QCoder judges are Anthropic models: claude-sonnet-4-20250514 for runs before April 2026 and claude-sonnet-4-6 afterwards. Claude Opus 4.6 has no QCoder run. Each sample is conditioned on the model’s prior attempts to reduce duplicates. Because this violates the i.i.d. assumption of the pass@ k k estimator, the values below describe the recorded sequential protocol rather than unbiased independent-sampling estimates.

Judge verdicts are not deterministic: identical code can receive different verdicts in separate judgment calls (QCoder example in Appendix E ). We measured neither inter-run nor cross-provider judge agreement, so QCoder results should be read as judge-dependent.

GPT-5 returns empty saved code for 316/755 QiskitHumanEval-Standard samples (41.9%), all scored as failures by pass@ k k . Of these, 315 stop at exactly 2,048 output tokens, which is consistent with the output budget being exhausted before any code is emitted. GPT-5’s empty-output rate grows on the suites with longer tasks: 41.9% on Standard, 53.0% on Hard, 55.0% on QuanBench-44, 59.5% on QuanBench-117, and 63.0% on QCoder. Table 13 reports nonempty and syntax-valid rates for every model. Low syntax validity is not confined to small models: Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.6 Flash produce syntactically valid code for only 53% and 59% of QuanBench-117 samples, and Gemini 3.1 Pro for only 58% of QCoder samples.

All 2,650 audited nonempty GPT-6 Astra outputs parse as Python, yet a substantial fraction fail evaluation. Saved execution fields and import diagnostics cannot yet serve as a validated infrastructure-adjusted execution-success rate, because candidate, reference, dependency, and evaluator failures have not been fully adjudicated.
